content.content:
Where a release's version comes from is this decision's whole subject, and it comes from one place: the release is handed the value as an explicit argument, and that argument is the only source. The value is one value, given at release time by whoever performs the release — not read out of the tree, not derived from the manifest's committed version, not computed from a date, a build counter or a branch name, not taken from a tag or from any other ambient fact of the repository, and not carried over from an earlier release. There is no second source and no fallback: a release given no value refuses rather than finding one, and it refuses before it packages anything, so a value that ships without having been given is a value the tree or the environment supplied.

The value is never committed. No committed file of the repository carries a release's version: not a manifest field, not a lockfile, not a changelog, not a generated document, not a node document, not a build configuration. A release writes the value it was given into the packaged artifact it produces and into nothing else of the tree, so the tree the release works in is the tree it found, save for that artifact: no file the run leaves behind other than the artifact carries it. A release may hold the value in a working file while it packs — stamping the manifest and restoring it is its own business — but it leaves no such file behind, and what the tree holds after the run is what it held before. The value is a fact of the release, not a fact of the repository, and the repository never holds it.

The manifest the extension is installed from still declares a version, because an installable manifest cannot omit one, and that committed field is not a release version. It holds whatever value the manifest's own decision fixes for the extension as it stands in the tree, and it keeps that value through a release: the release neither takes its value from that field — not when no argument is given, not as a default, not as a base to increment — nor writes the value it was given back into it. Which value the committed field holds, and why that value and no other, is settled where the manifest is settled, and nothing here fixes, restates or narrows it.

What this decision does not settle is everything around the value. The shape of the value — a plain triple, a prerelease or build channel, a dated stamp — is not fixed here; nor is how the argument is spelled, a positional value and a flag being alike an explicit argument; nor which program performs the release, what it packs with, what the artifact is called, or which steps it takes between the argument and the artifact. Those are the release's own commitments. Nor does this decision say what the extension is or how its page is composed: the extension is what its own decision records (uuutyrzs) and the page's composition is the composition's (tpztomkv), and neither is restated, narrowed or extended here.
content.rationale:
a packaged version is a release-time fact, and the tree is the one place it cannot live without going stale: the value that identifies a vsix is fixed at the moment it is packed, and every committed copy of it would be a second record of that moment that a later release has to remember to correct. Nothing in the repository can supply it either — packaging here is a local `npx vsce package` run by hand, with no CI environment to read a build number or a channel from, and a tag would need a naming convention that nothing in the repository records, so the value would be a guess read off whatever tag happened to be checked out. The explicit argument is the one source that needs no ambient state and no convention: whoever releases states the version, and the release refuses when they do not.

The prior art is deliberately not copied. The parent deccy CLI records its version in a node document and hand-stamps Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock, so the committed token is the version — right for a published crate, whose manifest is the artifact consumers resolve by version, and wrong here, where the version belongs to the packaged extension that is handed to the Marketplace and the manifest in the tree is only the document a development host installs. Copying that pattern would put the release number back in the tree, which is exactly what this decision forbids, and would leave the packaged version and the committed version free to disagree.

The commitment is stated as a rule about provenance, not a procedure, because the procedure is another node's: which value the manifest's committed field holds is fixed where the manifest is (its own decision owns the placeholder), and how the release is invoked, what it packs with and what it names the artifact are the release entry point's. What is settled here is only that the value arrives as an explicit argument, that it is one value, that nothing falls back to a committed or ambient source when the argument is absent, and that no committed file of the tree ever carries it — the rule the manifest's placeholder and the release entry point both take as given.
